Proving the product of two primitive polynomials in a UFD R[x] is primitive involves understanding the definitions and properties of primitive polynomials and the field of fractions.

First, recall that a polynomial f(x) in R[x] is primitive if its content (the greatest common divisor of its coefficients) is 1. In other words, f(x) has no non-trivial common factors among its coefficients.

Now, let f(x) and g(x) be two primitive polynomials in R[x]. We want to show that their product, h(x) = f(x)g(x), is also primitive.

Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that h(x) is not primitive. Then, there exists a non-trivial common divisor d of the coefficients of h(x). Since d divides all coefficients of h(x), it must also divide the coefficients of f(x) and g(x).

However, since f(x) and g(x) are primitive, their contents are 1. This means that the coefficients of f(x) and g(x) have no non-trivial common factors. Therefore, d must be 1, contradicting the assumption that d is a non-trivial common divisor of the coefficients of h(x).

Hence, we conclude that the product of two primitive polynomials in R[x] is indeed primitive.

Next, we want to show that if f and g are coprime in R[x], they are also coprime in F[x], the field of fractions.

Recall that two polynomials f(x) and g(x) are coprime if their greatest common divisor is 1. In R[x], this means that the content of f(x) and g(x) is 1.

Now, consider the field of fractions F[x] of R[x]. In F[x], the content of a polynomial is defined as the least common multiple of the contents of its coefficients. Since f(x) and g(x) are coprime in R[x], their contents are 1.

In F[x], the content of f(x) and g(x) is still 1, because the least common multiple of 1 is 1. Therefore, f(x) and g(x) are coprime in F[x].

In conclusion, the product of two primitive polynomials in a UFD R[x] is primitive, and if f and g are coprime in R[x], they are also coprime in F[x].
